research_question: When ancient and ancient-adjacent sources speak of the lost, reconstructed, found, housed, carried or consumed phallus of Osiris, what kind of evidence do they actually preserve: a biological relic, a local cult claim, a ritual simulacrum, a reliquary, a fish-as-receptacle motif, an Osirian effigy, or a textual body-part correspondence?
highest_admissible_current_claim: The source record preserves several distinct Osirian-phallus traditions. A late Greek witness says the organ was not recovered because three fish types consumed it and that Isis consecrated a replica; Egyptian ritual and temple traditions instead include recurrent discovery/reconstitution rites, named local relic-simulacra and reliquaries, including a strong Mendesian association with the phallus plus spine/back. No authenticated surviving biological tissue identifiable as the actual phallus of Osiris is established by this audit.

critical_reframing.old_search_question: Where is the literal missing phallus of Osiris?
critical_reframing.new_search_question: Which textual witnesses, local cults, relic-simulacra, reliquary vessels, fish cult objects, Osirian figurines and archaeological contexts carry the phallus-of-Osiris tradition, and which of them have secure provenance?
critical_reframing.reason: The evidence behaves like a distributed myth-ritual network rather than a single recoverable anatomical object.

evidence_hierarchy.TIER_A: Direct Egyptian texts, catalogued papyri, temple inscriptions, excavated objects with museum provenance, official museum/academic Egyptology records.
evidence_hierarchy.TIER_B: Peer-reviewed Egyptological synthesis based on primary Egyptian and classical sources.
evidence_hierarchy.TIER_C: Late classical authors such as Plutarch and Herodotus, preserved as historically important witnesses but not automatically projected backward as uniform pharaonic doctrine.
evidence_hierarchy.TIER_D: Modern retellings, tourism pages, blogs and fandom; discovery leads only.

source_ledger.date_context: Roman-period Greek author reporting Egyptian religious traditions
source_ledger.finding: Plutarch says the male member was the one part Isis did not find because it had been thrown into the river and eaten by lepidotus, phagrus and oxyrhynchus fish; Isis then made a replica and consecrated the phallus.
source_ledger.use: Important late witness for LOST_IN_WATER + FISH_CONSUMPTION + REPLICA_CONSECRATION.
source_ledger.limits: Not a direct pharaonic-period Egyptian text and should not erase Egyptian local variants.

source_ledger.finding: The Met notes Plutarch's link between lepidotus and consumption of Osiris's phallus but explicitly cautions that Plutarch's understanding of the story can be questioned.
source_ledger.use: NEGATIVE_CANARY against treating the Plutarch version as universal Egyptian doctrine.

source_ledger.finding: In the body-part deity correspondences of Book of the Dead 42, the phallus of the transformed deceased is identified with Osiris.
source_ledger.use: Shows an Egyptian ritual-textual association PHALLUS <-> OSIRIS independent of the Plutarch fish narrative.
source_ledger.limits: This is theological body correspondence, not evidence for location of a physical relic.

source_ledger.finding: Comparative Khoiak ritual schedules include episodes described as finding parts of Osiris; the phallus appears among the parts found on different festival days in different source traditions. Seeded-earth Osiris figures were produced, buried, replaced and ritually handled across Egyptian temples.
source_ledger.use: Strong evidence that FINDING_THE_PHALLUS can be a recurrent ritual operation, not necessarily a claim that one unique flesh relic was physically rediscovered.
source_ledger.limits: Festival synchronization and local variation must be retained.

source_ledger.finding: Peer-reviewed Egyptological synthesis: the Osirian phallus functions as a symbol of virility, fecundity, integrity and restored power; Egyptian traditions include replacement/reconstruction, fish-receptacle motifs, phallic amulets, Osirian effigies, processional relic-simulacra and local cult claims.
source_ledger.use: Primary synthesis for separating anatomical myth, funerary restoration and cult-object evidence.

source_ledger.finding: From the Late Period, Dendera representations attest veneration of Osirian phallus relic-simulacra in multiple nomes; processions carried such relics in anthropomorphic- or ram-headed reliquary vessels.
source_ledger.use: Converts the search from one missing object to a RELIC_SIMULACRUM_NETWORK.

source_ledger.finding: Spieser reports that at Mendes the Osirian phallus is called the 'copulating Ba' and is associated with the god's divine flesh consisting of the virile member and spine/back; it is integrated with djed/spinal symbolism and female resurrection figures.
source_ledger.use: Highest-priority textual target for the Mendes branch.

source_ledger.finding: Djedet, Greek Mendes, is the principal city of Lower Egyptian nome 16 and the temple center of Banebdjedet, whose four souls include Osiris.
source_ledger.use: Geographical correction and cult-context anchor for the Mendes phallus/spine tradition.

source_ledger.finding: British Museum confirms the Mendesian nome as the 16th nome of Lower Egypt, centered on Tell el-Ruba/Mendes.
A Late Period-Ptolemaic lepidotus fish object is explicitly catalogued as connected in mythology to Seth's dismemberment of Osiris.
source_ledger.use: Material-culture witness for fish symbolism, not a physical phallus relic.

source_ledger.finding: The schilbe fish was represented on the standard of Mendes and closely associated with the local goddess Hatmehyt.
source_ledger.use: Important control: not every Mendes fish object belongs to the Osiris-phallus-eating fish story. Local fish cults must be species/context separated.

source_ledger.finding: Osirian figurine catacombs are reported at Karnak and Oxyrhynchos; Khoiak-type Osirian figures could be buried in dedicated necropoleis and in some contexts deposited into sacred lakes or the river.
source_ledger.use: Creates an archaeological search class for ritual Osirian deposits, but not a claim that any such figure is the literal missing organ.

candidate_geographies.why_priority: Papyrus Brooklyn 47.218.84 and later Egyptological synthesis associate the Osirian virile member with the spine/back and a 'copulating Ba' in the Mendesian theological system; the city is independently established as a major Banebdjedet-Osiris cult context.
candidate_geographies.do_not_claim: No current evidence that an actual preserved biological phallus is present at the site.

candidate_geographies.why_priority: Roof-chapel Khoiak inscriptions and processional imagery preserve detailed local relic/simulacrum systems and body-part finding schedules.
candidate_geographies.do_not_claim: Ritual 'finding' is not literal excavation coordinates for a biological organ.

candidate_geographies.why_priority: The oxyrhynchus/mormyrid fish becomes one major receiver/consumer motif in late accounts and Osirian figurine catacombs are archaeologically attested in the area.
candidate_geographies.do_not_claim: Fish symbolism does not identify a unique fish, skeleton or tissue sample as Osiris's organ.

candidate_geographies.why_priority: Spieser citing Beinlich reports a phallus-and-testicles relic tradition in the 7th nome of Upper Egypt.

false_positive_controls.reason: Min is independently ithyphallic and can be mistaken for Osirian phallic iconography if crown/body/context are ignored.
A phallus-form amulet can restore or protect sexual function without representing the unique phallus of Osiris.
Mendes has its own fish-standard/goddess context unrelated to the three fish of Plutarch's consumption story.
An ithyphallic Osiris figure or corn mummy is a ritual whole/body simulacrum, not automatically a relic container.
A Greek/Roman literary account can preserve a real tradition while still differing from Egyptian temple and funerary sources.

phase_1_text: Acquire direct catalogue/scan/edition metadata for Papyrus Brooklyn 47.218.84.
Extract Dendera roof-chapel passages that name the phallus relic, its nome, vessel and paired body part.
Build a source-separated matrix: Egyptian temple text vs funerary text vs Greek/Roman witness vs modern synthesis.
phase_2_objects: Collect museum objects explicitly catalogued as Osiris phallus/relic/reliquary, not merely generic erotic or fertility objects.
Collect matched Min, generic phallic amulet and fish-standard controls.
Require museum object number, provenance, excavation/findspot where available, period, material, inscription status and image receipt.
phase_3_geography: Resolve Mendes/Tell el-Ruba temple-sector evidence from excavation reports.
Resolve Kenem/UE7 local relic place-name before plotting or archaeology claims.
Separate Oxyrhynchos fish-cult evidence from Osirian-catacomb evidence.
phase_4_claim_test: Ask whether any object has a secure chain that moves beyond SIMULACRUM/RELIQUARY to claimed biological human tissue.
If none does, freeze NO_AUTHENTICATED_BIOLOGICAL_RELIC as a negative certificate rather than inventing a missing-object hunt.
If a candidate appears, require independent archaeological publication, material analysis and provenance before promotion.

creative_branch_link.rule: In the Kem story, the boy may catch a fish carrying the missing organ because this is explicit alternate fiction inspired by the fish-consumption motif. In research, no such unique fish or recoverable organ is assumed.
